issues.legal_issue: An accomplice’s testimony may support a conviction when it is reliable and is corroborated in material particulars connecting each accused with the crime.
material_facts: The approver had participated in the criminal activities and killings described by the prosecution.
The approver gave evidence about the killings of three victims in one incident and three other victims in separate incidents.

Independent witnesses, including eyewitnesses to the attacks, supported material parts of his account; other evidence included recoveries, identification evidence, medical evidence and circumstances surrounding the killings and disposal of the bodies.
The courts below had examined the evidence and found the approver’s account reliable and sufficiently corroborated.
issues.conclusion: The approver’s testimony, supported by independent evidence in material particulars, was safe to act upon and established the relevant appellants’ guilt in the killings to which his evidence related.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Evidence Act, an accomplice is a competent witness and conviction on uncorroborated accomplice evidence is not illegal, but settled practice requires the evidence to be reliable and sufficiently corroborated. Corroboration must be independent, material and connect or tend to connect each accused with the crime; it need not independently prove the offence or confirm every circumstance. The Court relied on Sarwan Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab, Lachhi Ram v. State of Punjab, Mohd. Husain Umar Kochra v. K.S. Dalipsinghji, Ravinder Singh v. State of Haryana, Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan, Tribhuvan Nath v. State of Maharashtra and Vemireddy Satyanarayan Reddy v. State of Hyderabad.

predicates.criminal_appeal_review: The court is reviewing convictions in a criminal appeal.
predicates.accomplice_testimony_reliable: An accomplice gave testimony that the court found reliable.
predicates.independent_material_corroboration_conne: Independent evidence supported material parts of the accomplice’s account and connected the accused with the crime.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal involves reliable accomplice testimony supported by independent material evidence connecting the accused with the crime, the testimony is sufficient to support a conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A retracted judicial confession may be acted upon when it was voluntary and true and receives sufficient independent corroboration in material particulars.
material_facts: Two accused made judicial confessions before magistrates and later retracted them.
The magistrates gave evidence about the precautions taken in recording the confessions, and the courts found the confessions voluntary.
The confessions described the accused’s participation in the killings and related events.

Witness testimony, recoveries, forensic and medical evidence, and circumstances concerning the victims’ last appearances and the disposal or discovery of their bodies supported material parts of the confessions.
issues.conclusion: The retracted confessions were true and voluntary and sufficiently corroborated; they could be acted upon and supported the findings of guilt against the confessing accused.
issues.legal_principle: A confession must be a direct acknowledgement of guilt and must be voluntary, meaning it was not caused by inducement, threat or promise. A retracted judicial confession must be true and, as a rule of prudence, receive sufficient corroboration in material particulars from independent evidence. Corroboration of every circumstance is unnecessary; general corroboration of important incidents may suffice. The Court relied on Balbir Singh v. State of Punjab, Sarwan Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab, Ediga Anamma v. State of A.P. and State of U.P. v. Boota Singh.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_review and judicial_confession_retracted and confession_voluntary_and_true and independent_material_corroboration

predicates.criminal_appeal_review: The court is reviewing a conviction in a criminal appeal.
predicates.judicial_confession_retracted: An accused made a judicial confession and later withdrew or denied it.
predicates.confession_voluntary_and_true: The court found that the confession was freely made and was true.
predicates.independent_material_corroboration: Independent evidence supported important parts of the confession.

issues.definition: A retracted judicial confession may support a conviction when it was voluntary and true and independent evidence corroborates it in material particulars.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory protection for communications between spouses does not prevent testimony about a confession when the witness was not the accused’s legally wedded spouse.
material_facts: A witness testified that an accused had told her about the killings.
The witness was living as the accused’s mistress and was not his legally wedded wife; his marriage to another woman remained subsisting.
The courts below found that the witness’s relationship with the accused did not constitute a marriage attracting the claimed protection.
issues.conclusion: The witness’s testimony was not excluded by Section 122 of the Evidence Act because she was not the accused’s legally wedded spouse.
issues.legal_principle: Section 122 of the Evidence Act did not apply on these facts because the witness was the accused’s mistress rather than his legally wedded wife. The Court upheld the factual finding that the provision was not attracted.

predicates.criminal_appeal_review: The court is reviewing a criminal appeal in which testimony is challenged as protected marital communication.
predicates.witness_testifies_to_spousal_communicati: A witness testified about a communication made by the accused in their relationship.
predicates.witness_not_legally_wedded_spouse: The witness was not legally married to the accused.

issues.definition: When a witness testifies about a communication but was not legally married to the accused, the testimony is not excluded by the spousal communication protection.

issues.legal_issue: The death penalty is justified only in a rarest-of-rare case in which the aggravating circumstances, considered with the offender’s circumstances and any mitigation, make a lesser sentence inadequate.
material_facts: The accused whose death sentences were upheld were found to have taken part in several planned, brutal killings and in concealing or disposing of the bodies.
The evidence showed organised criminal activity, repeated elimination of people regarded as obstructing that activity, and especially cruel and calculated conduct.

The Court considered the circumstances of the crimes and offenders, the roles and participation of the accused, and the proposed mitigating circumstances, including claimed distress and other explanations.
The Court found the relevant accused’s conduct exceptionally cruel and depraved and found the crimes and offenders presented a grave danger to society.
issues.conclusion: The death sentences imposed on the two accused whose participation was established by their own corroborated confessions and other evidence were confirmed as warranted in rarest-of-rare cases.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 354(3) and 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, life imprisonment is the rule and death the exception; the court must give special reasons and consider both the crime and the criminal, weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances. Death is reserved for the gravest cases of extreme culpability where the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed. The Court relied on Jagmohan Singh v. State of U.P., Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration), Mangal Singh v. State of U.P., Ediga Anamma v. State of A.P. and Allauddin Mian v. State of Bihar.

rule.if: capital_sentence_appeal and multiple_planned_brutal_killings and exceptional_cruelty_or_depravity and offender_presents_serious_social_danger and mitigating_circumstances_do_not_make_lesser_sentence_adequate

predicates.capital_sentence_appeal: The court is reviewing a death sentence in a criminal appeal.
predicates.multiple_planned_brutal_killings: The offender participated in multiple planned and brutal killings.
predicates.exceptional_cruelty_or_depravity: The manner and circumstances of the crimes showed exceptional cruelty or depravity.
predicates.offender_presents_serious_social_danger: The court found that the offender’s conduct showed a serious continuing danger to society.
predicates.mitigating_circumstances_do_not_make_les: The court considered the offender’s mitigating circumstances and found that they did not make a lesser sentence adequate.

issues.definition: A death sentence is warranted when a capital-sentence appeal concerns multiple planned and brutal killings, exceptional cruelty or depravity, and a serious social danger, and mitigation does not make a lesser sentence adequate.

issues.legal_issue: A death sentence must be assessed individually, and it should not be imposed when the evidence about the accused’s particular participation is not sufficiently safe or strong to justify that extreme penalty.
material_facts: One accused was convicted of murder on evidence supporting common intention, including the approver’s testimony and corroborating evidence.
The evidence of the approver about this accused’s precise participation in two killings contained a discrepancy about whether he held a victim’s legs.
The only evidence describing that accused’s particular role in those killings was the approver’s evidence; there was no other evidence of the precise nature of his participation.
The co-accused’s retracted confessions implicated him, but the Court declined to use those confessions to assess his individual participation for the death-sentence decision.
The Court distinguished his evidence and role from those of the two accused whose death sentences it upheld.
issues.conclusion: The accused’s murder convictions and other sentences were confirmed, but his death sentence was reduced to imprisonment for life because the evidence of his particular participation was not sufficiently safe to justify the extreme sentence.
issues.legal_principle: The sentencing court must consider the role of each offender and the quality of the evidence bearing on that role, while weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances. A co-accused’s confession cannot be used to determine the nature of another accused’s individual participation for deciding whether to impose death. The Court relied on Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and, on the significance of evidentiary quality at sentencing, Dudh Nath Pandey v. State of U.P. and Suresh v. State of U.P.

predicates.capital_sentence_appeal: The court is reviewing a death sentence in a criminal appeal.
predicates.individual_role_evidence_uncertain_or_we: The evidence of the accused’s particular participation was uncertain or insufficiently strong, even though evidence supported the conviction.
predicates.death_sentence_assessment_depends_on_tha: The accused’s particular role and the quality of evidence about it are relevant to whether the extreme sentence is justified.

issues.definition: When a death-sentence appeal turns on an accused’s particular role and the evidence of that role is uncertain or weak, the death sentence is reduced to life imprisonment.

issues.legal_issue: A sentencing hearing requirement is met when the trial court questions each convicted accused about sentence and considers the answers before choosing the punishment.
material_facts: After recording convictions, the trial judge specifically questioned each accused about sentence and recorded the answers.
The trial judge considered those answers, reviewed the relevant sentencing decisions, and considered the role of each accused and aggravating and mitigating circumstances before imposing sentence.
issues.conclusion: The trial court complied with Section 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the challenge alleging non-compliance was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Section 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the court, after conviction, to hear the accused on sentence. On the facts, the individual questioning and consideration of the answers satisfied that requirement.

predicates.criminal_appeal_review: The court is reviewing a criminal conviction and sentence on appeal.
predicates.each_convicted_accused_questioned_on_sen: After conviction, the trial court asked each accused about the sentence to be imposed.
predicates.answers_considered_before_sentence: The trial court considered the accused’s answers before selecting the sentences.

issues.definition: The sentencing hearing requirement is satisfied when every convicted accused is questioned after conviction and the court considers the answers before imposing sentence.
